name: Question 6
problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4 \\ L{{e}^{-4t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4},\,s>-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s+4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4)+(s-4)}{(s-4)(s+4)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)}$ is defined for

$$
(4,\infty )\cap (-4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

First, recall that, by definition cosh⁡(4t)=e4t+e−4t2.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

L{cosh⁡(4t)}=L{e4t+e−4t2}=L{e4t2+e−4t2}=L{e4t2}+L{e−4t2}=12L{e4t}+12L{e−4t}.

Now, we recall that L{ekt}=1s−k,s>k.

Therefore, we have the following: L{e4t}=1s−4,s>4L{e−4t}=1s+4,s>−4

Therefore, the Laplace transform of cosh⁡(4t) is

L{cosh⁡(4t)}=12L{e4t}+12L{e−4t}=12⋅1s−4+12⋅1s+4=12(1s−4+1s+4)=12((s+4)+(s−4)(s−4)(s+4))=12(2ss2−16)=ss2−16.

Finally, since L{e4t} is defined for s∈(4,∞) and L{e−4t} is defined for s∈(−4,∞), we have that L{cosh⁡(4t)} is defined for (4,∞)∩(−4,∞)=(4,∞), that is, s>4.
